newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-Dairy Farm says repositioning hit profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dairy Farm says repositioning hit profits.

text.p: Retailer Dairy Farm International Holdings Ltd on Tuesday blamed repositioning costs in Australia and Britain for a 79 percent plunge in 1996 net attributable profit to US$27.9 million.
But the group's 1997 performance should benefit from the absence of such costs, the company said.
"We are creating a sound base for renewed profit growth, and in 1997 we will benefit from the absence of non-recurring repositioning costs," chairman Simon Keswick said in a statement.

Dairy Farm, which is based in Hong Kong but listed in Singapore, said it spent US$77.5 million on repositioning provisions for its Franklins chain in Australia and its Kwik Save Plc operation in Britain.
New "Fresh" stores in Australia had been well accepted, and it was speeding up the conversion of its "No Frills" operations, it said.
Repositioning provisions, however, would continue to restrain Franklins' profit recovery for the next two years, the company said.
Its Kwik Save chain had embarked on a three-year programme of rationalising and repositioning its stores.
Despite the profit fall, the group said it was paying a final dividend of 4.35 U.S. cents a share, unchanged from 1995.
Edouard Ettedgui, a spokesman for Dairy Farm Management Services Ltd, said the group's decision to leave the dividend unchanged despite the profit slide reflected optimism about the outlook.
"We are confident about the outlook," Ettedgui told Reuters by telephone. He said it was normal to have a dividend policy "which does not follow the volatility or otherwise of the earnings".
After paying out dividends, the company ended with a loss of US$77.4 million against a US$31.7 million gain in 1995.

Competition was strong in Taiwan where hypermarkets had taken a significant market share, and its Wellcome supermarket chain reported a decline in profit. Its Mannings drugstore chain traded at a loss, the group said, releasing its result.
However its Woolworths chain in New Zealand had continued to perform strongly in 1996, it said.
In Hong Kong, it achieved "steady sales and profit growth" with its Wellcome and Mannings chains, Dairy Farm said.
Maxim's Caterers, a 50 percent restaurant associate had "another excellent year", with sales and profit growth well ahead of the industry trend in Hong Kong, Dairy Farm said.
"The company now has over 300 (Maxim's) outlets in Asia, and its prospects remain outstanding," Dairy Farm said.

Dairy Farm is 52 percent owned by Jardine Strategic Holdings Ltd, a holding company for Asian conglomerate Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd. Jardine Matheson and Jardine Strategic are due to report annual profits on Thursday.
